in June, 1922. They continued to live

Nixon has battled for life without
arms. She Is the daughter of Mr..
and Mrs. T. J. Nixon, Of this city.


At the time of her birth Ellen
Lorraine's shoulders bore two tiny
dimples where her arms should
have. been. Today the smooth,
white skin has filled out, hiding
even the dimples and leaving the
otherwise perfectly formed baby
without a sign Of arms.


Mrs. Nixon says she cried night
and day for weeks when she first
heard of the plight of her new
born baby.


The tears are dried now. however,
and the mother has dedicated her
life to making the baby efficient in
manipulating things with her feet.


Nature, always ready to tighten
the load of her afflicted children,
has 80 formed the baby's hips that
she can reach the top of her head
with her feet, using no apparent
effort.


Already the child has learned to
hold objects between her toes.


The child's feet are rapidly as
suming the delicate. sensitive APP
pearance Of hands. She uses them

claiming Viscount Goto was blamable

STEUBENvILLE, Ohio, October 10.
The home OF Charles Pearce, thir-
ty-six, prohibition enforcement officer
at Smithfield. Ohio, west of here, was
blown up today by dynamite. Pearce,
his wife and baby escaped serious
injury.


The blast partially wrecked the
city hall opposite the Pearce home,
the Spragg restaurant, the home of
Mrs. Mary Merryman. and broke win
dows in threescore residences.


The dynamite, placed under the
front of Pearce's house, wrecked the
structure. and it collapsed inward.
the walls and roof falling into the
basement. Pearce, his wife and sew
enteen- n-month-old baby, were thrown
into the cellar with the debris.


Digs Wife From Ruins.


Pearce extricated himself, rescued
his baby, and then, with the aid of
neIshbors, dug his wife from the
ruins after an hours hard work. The
baby was cut and bruised. Mrs
Pearce had her back injured and suf-
fered greatly from shock.


Mrs. Merryman's home adjoining
was so badly wrecked that the aged
lady, who had been seriously i'll, had
to be removed from the tottering
structure with ladders to the second
floor. The damage caused by the ex-
plosion is estimated in excess Of
$4,000.


Miners en- route to work claim to
have seen four strangers standing at
a corner near the Pearce home, and
others report they saw an automobile
with several man passengers leaving
the town at a high rate of speed
shortly before the blast


Got Bootleggers' Threats.


Sheriff Ed. Lucas and deputies of
Jefferson county are working on the
theory that liquor law violators pros
ecuted by Pearce were responsible for
the outrage, and, according to latest
reports, are seeking suspects at Piney
Fork, a mining town near Smithfield.


Pearce claims he has received no
threatening letters, but has been
openly threatened by bootleggers ar
rested recently.

Within few feet of where her

yesterday afternoon at Chapel Point,

deep. Her parents. Mr.. and Mrs.
Charles B. Scott, 631 Alabama avenue.
Congress Heights, were seated on a
bench overlooking the river and Lois
Stebbing, her chum and schoolmate
was only a few feet away.


Ellen Scott, sufferer from paralysis.
had been crippled since childhood and
Lois Stebbing. fifteen years old, 3217
Nichols avenue, had been her school
companion the past several years, fire.
quently carrying her books to school.


Yesterday, about IL o'clock, members
of the Scott family and Ellen's chum
left the Scott home and motored to
Chapel Point, and il was about 3 AS
o'clock in the afternoon when the acci-
dent happened. Mr.. and Mrs. Scott had
finished their bathing, changed their
clothing and were enjoying the breezes
from the river at point from which
they could watch those who were in
the water.


The father had been near his child
drowned. Miss Stebbing had gone, to
deeper water. leaving Ellen near the
shore where she was wading in shallow
water.


Ellen lost her footing and fell and
was in the water only a short while
before other bathers went to her as
sistance, Lois Stebbing discovering her
lying in the water and calling for help.
Life was extinct when the body was
taken from the water and the body was
brought home.


The deceased is survived by her
parents and an eight-year-old sister,
Alice. Funeral services will be held at
the Scott home at O'Clock Wednesday
afternoon.

BERLIN, November 20.-The threat
Of a general famine overhangs that
inferno which is called the Ruhr dis
trict, for employers. reich and French
alike having repudiated responsible
ity either for feeding or employing
its four million inhabitants after No
vember 80.


The writer has just returned from
the Ruhr, which he entered with a
German friend through "smugglers
der which the French sentries have
neglected. Our guide was a straight
forward youngster. formerly mine
clerk, but now unemployed, who is
smuggling cigarettes for living.
The Ruhr landscape Is strikingly
changed. Where formerly the Ruhr
had no canopy of sky but only black
smoke for a roof. now the hundreds
of smokestacks which encircle one
at any point are smokeless. Huge
peared vaguely gray through the
smoke. now loom UP black.


Feeble Business I'm Shops.


The Ruhr, despite the partial ac-
tivity Of certain works like the Krupp
plants, unproductive repair works and
the feeble business done In the shops.
Is virtually dead. Telephones and
In Dortmund the streets are lined
with iron shutters, protecting the
shops against plundering. Enormous
crowds wander aimlessly about. The
vast space before the railway station
Is black with humanity crawling
They are the BLACK stock exchange"
which is a feature Of every city In
the Ruhr since the occupation. Here
the Germans must buy francs for rail-
way fares, since the Franco-Belgian
administration accepts only francs.
but sells them only at the rate of 80
to 100 per cent over normal.


Here also is the thieves market. 1t
is the shadiest looking crowd of
humanity ever assembled in any
thing stealable - shoes. watches,
beads, cigarettes, horsewhips.


From the street above come several
thousand unemployed. marching in
folk songs with admirable harmony.
They join the miscellaneous masses
below.


For a moment, silence. Then-panic.


The police have attacked.


Door Is Barricnded.


A woman with baby carriage
dashes past the writer Into the sta
ton, but French troops bar the doors,
cutting off this means of escape,
while platoons of troops take up the
guard outside.


Two French armored cars with
faded camoufiage rumble through the
streets.


The "black exchange" resume es
business. A policeman says to the
writer:


"Yes, it happens every day. 1 don't
blame them, they are hungry. Their
dole buys an average of two loaves
of bread a week. No, there has not
been much trouble here"


He forgets to mention that there
has been a skirmish that very morn
ing in which one was killed and sew
eral were wounded.


When the writer arrived at Essen
two hours later the city showed the
usual hopeless Indifference, although
there had been barricade fighting in
which a dozen had been killed and
many wounded that afternoon. The
unemployed had resisted the police
with rocks. while the few that had
firearms had seized a part of the
Krupp works.

MOBILE, Ala, October 23.-Fears
that unidentified ships, together with
all on board, may have perished in
the recent heavy winds and seas
which swept the gulf are expressed
in maritime circles, following the re-
port of Capt. c. II. Daughrill of the
tug Lytle that he had sighted masses
of wreckage floating in the gulf on
his scouting tour for vessels in dis
tress.


Torn and twisted spars, timbers
and hulls, apparently wrecked within
the past few days, were being tossed
on heavy seas resulting from the
gulf disturbance all the way from
Pensacola to Chandelur Island, Capt.
Daughrill reported.


Saw Body Floating.


Capt. Daughrill also reported sight
the gulf some miles from Perdido
bay. The body was believed by Capt.
Daughrill to be that of one of the
victims of the Bluefields wreck.


The Lytle was sent on a scouting
tour of the gulf late last week, fol-
lowing the storm, by F. w. Crenshaw,
manager of the Gulf Towing and
Wrecking Company, and has just re-
turned to Mobile. Capt. Daughrill
reported that the seas were very
heavy when he first went out into
the gulf, but that they had now be-
come calm.


Ship Found Refuge.


The Lytle went to Chandelur Island,
Ship Island and all along the Missis-
sippt coast and then turned eastward
south of Pensacola and back to Mo-
bile again. One English schooner
commanded by Capt. Steele, the Ma
pletield, was found behind Ship Island,
where she had taken refuge from the
storm. She was from Antilla, Cuba,
uninJured, and was towed into Mobile.
The Echo and the coast guard cut
ter Tallapoosa were also out in the
gulf scouting for ships in distress
The Echo returned, but the Talla-
poosa has not been heard from since
she left Mobile last Thursday morn
ing. Plans for the rescue of the
schooner Rachel. beached forty feet
from deep water four miles east of
Fort Morgan by the storm, were
made and the task was found so diff
cult that the owner of the ship, W. 3.
Paterson, is undecided whether to
attempt the feat.

hind it, used by members of the crew

met death in this car. They were its

NEW YORK, Feb. S-The pirates
who swarmed at the command of
John Silver and flew the jolly Roger
for Captain Kidd are not to be rele-
gated to the motion picture screen
or the illustrations of nursery books.


They are living at large and at
their trade, scanning the high seas
for their hapless victims, but their
prize is not jewels nor Spanish doub-
ICONS, but that much rarer article,
real liquor, which skirts the coast
of the American Sahara on it's way
to more pleasant chimes.


Pettipass, rear admiral of the rum
navy, tells a tale which puts Stew
enson and Jeffrey Farnol in a class
with Jane Austen. His flagship, the
Marion Mosher, left New York De-
cember 81 with the capstan free and
the wind alec and her matches bat
tened tight over her precious cargo
from a wine company, under bond
for delivery in ST. Johns, New
Brunswick, Canada. She arrived at
ST. Johns still afloat and her crew
intact, but her holds were empty
and her cargo gone. The log which
Pettipass kept through all the stress
Of battle gives the story.


Well off the coast of Long Island,
at daybreak, the lookout reported u
low black hull, some miles off the
starboard quarter, but closing fast.
Fearing interference with his Valu-
able shipment, Pettipass ordered full
speed ahead, but no effort aVailed
against the hawk-like stranger, which
came on with a bone in her teeth.


AT the distance of normal visibility
she flew a challenging pennant, and
the Marion Mosher raised her flags of
registry and destination. Then,
to the Mortified eyes, the black en-.
sign and white skull, or something
like that, fluttered to the pursuing
masthead and long-range guns from
concealed turretS, or something like
that, swung slowly in their direc-
ton.


The crew of the unfortunate
freightcr could not believe the grim
sight was real until puff of
smoke from the left bow rifle fol-
lowed by a splash a hundred feet
across their bow and the muffled re-
port of the shot, told the enemy
meant business.


Yielding to the irresistible, Petit.
pass rang down his engines and the
black craft closed aboard.


The log hints in stilted terms of
the bitter scenes that followed. How
the pirate crew demanded uncondi-
tiOnaI surrender of all the MOsher
carried, which was a confiscat ted
cargo, reloaded: of the grief of strong
men watching strong liquor taken
forever from them; of bottles torn by
force from their cases. and cases
parted from their barrels.

walls.

American warships in Turkish
waters will continue their station
there and take no part in the dis.
pute between the Turkish and allied
governments, which has brought
threats of bombardment, it was
stated officially here today.


The American naval forces now
in Turkish waters comprise the
United States Cruiser Pittsburgh,
the converted yacht Scorpion and
twenty destroyers.


The Pittsburgh and thirteen OF
the destroyers were at Constan-
tinople, one destroyer, the Edsall,
was at Smyrna, and the other six
were scattered at various ports,
according to last reports received
at the Navy Department here. The
Pittsburgh is Admiral Longs flag.
ship. Admiral Long being the rank
ing American official in that region
during the absence of Admiral Mark
Bristol at the Lausanne conference.


Officials declared they anticipated
no difficulty between the Angora
and allied governments that could
possibly involve the American war
ships. The destroyers were sent
over last November to assist in
refugee work, ana rendered notable
service in this regard.


The Turkish order for allied war
ships to leave the harbor Is not inter
preted here as referring to the Ameri-
can destroyers now on duty there.
Officials said the Angora govern.
ment was fully cognizant that the
small force of American naval
strength IN Turkish waters was there
on peaceful business, and the Turk
ish ultimatum was construed by Of
ficials here as referring only to the
larger war vessels Of the allied
powers,

ESSEN, March 6-The French
have advanced from Nohwinkle rail-
road junction and penetrated south
around the British zone to Greafrath
and Kronenberg and have reached
Wipperfurth. Thus they have al
Germany and have cut all the rail
lines leading from Cologne to unoc-
cupied Germany.


There is much speculation regard
ing the reasons for the advance. Many
think that the British are preparing
to leave the Rhine and that the French
are getting ready to occupy Cologne
as soon IS the British leave. 1t is con-
sidered significant that the British
have suspended sick leave absences
of soldiers and officers-something not
done before in the three years of the
occupation.


The French have not entered Bar
men or Elberfeld important dye
cities. but have cut them off from rail
connection with unoccupied Germany.


Without police Essen has become a
mecca for Germany's thieves, and
not a night passes without daring
hold-up OF burglary. Bandits entered
the finest cabaret in the city last
night when night life was at its
gayest. with champagne flowing.
dancing and late dining. The in
truders robbed the guests and cleaned
out the checkroom before they were
driven away by fremen. who are try
ing to replace the police. Three of
the bandits were captured.
Several shops have been plundered
by the toughs from the mining dis
tricts and other hard characters from
Hamburg


Residents of Essen leave their
money and watches at home, for the
feeling of insecurity is general and
few venture into the dark streets.
The Berlin government has forbidden
the replacing of the police disarmed
and expelled by the French.


Cases have been reported Of French
troops robbing pedestrians, and a
French colonel has arrived to investi-
gate such complaints.

DUBLIN, February 2l.--An organ
lied attack was made this afternoon
on various government officials in
Dublin. An attempt also was made
to set the income tax office on fire.
National troops, guarding the local
government board office, fired and
killed one irregular and captured
three others.


Three government offices were
raided simultaneously. Some of the
attackers attempted to set the build
ings on fire. while others kept up a
rain Of bullets from their positions on
adjoining roofs.


The motor car used by the irregu-
lars attacking the central office was
captured by the government forces
and was found to contain land mines.


The fighting caused intense excite
ment among the population.


When the attacks commenced many
people were on their way from their
offices and places of business to lunch,
and the firing caused a general STAN
pede. Tram cars were abandoned, the
streets cleared and the fire brigade
turned out.

TREAT FALLS, Mont.-Three


" tiny silver-black foxes opened


their eyes at the Great Falls
fox farm, on the outskirts of this
city, recently, and found that for
nine days they had been receiving
nourishment not from their own
mothers but from two cats, both
Of which had kittens the day the
foxes were born. And, what's
more, George Woolf, superin-
tendent of the fox farm, has
fooled the mother cats for nine
days, and they are still in the
land of the innocent.


At their birth the full filters of
kittens were hastily removed and
the three fox pups substituted.
The cat mothers never noticed the
difference and have been tenderly
nursing the foxes, licking their
glossy black backs, for days.


The two mother cats rest in the
warm sunshine in a barrel, with
the fox pups, and contentedly
meow. To the onlooker there is
little difference between the
motherless kittens and the pups
a single touch of silver gray on
the tails Of the baby foxes alone
distinguishing them from the
kittens.


According to Superintendent
Woolf-what's in a name at a fox
farm, anyway-cats make good
mothers. He said that often when
kittens are taken away from cats
they run into the open, adopting
the offspring Of rabbits and
gophers to fill the mother instinct.


The Great Falls farm now
boasts. eleven full-grown and
thirty baby foxes, and the stork
Is on the way with additional off
spring. Food of the animals con-
sists Of prepared biscuits, eggs,
horse meat, and young gophers
and rabbits.

Sahara, regions strikingly different
from the sand dune sections, that are
the homes of the fierce Tuaregs-the
real people of the desert"-who have
constantly preyed on the camel cara
vans that Arabs and Jews have sent
periodically from the Mediterranean
toward Central Africa.


Tuaregs, Land Buccaneers.


These people, natives and rulers Of
the middle desert, are the allies of no
one, but wage furtive guerrilla war
fare with all who invade their inhos-
pitable domain. They are land buc-
cancers, forever at war with all civil
ization and its restraints. Masked
Tuaregs are Berber nomads, white
desert people, whose country Is prob
ably the most inaccessible on earth.
Even before Egyptian civilization be
gan to leave coherent records of Its
history, the Tuaregs, or Berbers, were
long established along Northern Africa.
The great Arab invasion of the
Eleventh century displaced them from
their possessions upon the seacoast
and drove them into the savage area Of
the interior desert, where, with their
hands raised against all who come into
their pathless country, they have
maintained themselves through the in
tervening centuries, despite paucity of
water, dust storms, and lack of farming
land, requisitioning by force of arms
from the Arabs and Egyptians, to the
north and east, and from the blacks
Of the Soudan, in the south, such. neces-
sites and luXurles as their cheerless
portion of mother earth cannot supply
them.


There are five main tribes in the
Tuareg confederation, and they inhabit
the desert from Tuat to Timbuktu and
from Fezzan to Finder. These fierce
adventures who have forced the great
desolation to yield them a support
number 100000 or more, according to
estimate; and they have made them
selves feared by the natives from the
Mediterranean to the jungles of Cen
trail Africa.


The Tuaregs wear the end of their
turban cloth drawn around the face,
allowing nothing but the eyes to be
seen. 1t is worn for the purpose of
protecting the throat and lungs from
the cutting blasts of fine desert sand,
and also, probably, as an element en-
hancing the mystery of their life, for
they seldom or never remove these
masks, whether rowing over the desert
or visiting in the cities on the coast
Due to these cloths, they are called
Masked Tuaregs, while the Arabs call
them People of the Veil" The masks
are dark blue and white, the former
being worn by Tuareg mobiles and the
latter by the serfs and slaves.


Some centers for trade, Tuareg
towns, are situated in the middle
desert. However, the Tuareg has little
cares for trade and industry. He Is a
fearless, enduring, hard-fighting ad-
venturer along the merchandise trails
that cross the desert. Sometimes. a
single caravan consists of thousands of
camels and merchandise to the value
of hundreds of thousands of dollars.


The Tuaregs are of the purest Ber-
ber stock, the noble families unmixed
with other blood, and, in their own Ian
guage, they call themselves 1.-The noble
people" Nominally, they are Moham-
medans, and some of their number
compose the most intolerant and war
like sect in Islam, the Senussite sect.
Their hatred for the foreigner is great
er even than that bred by their religion
and so they are more exclusive than
ever were the Chinese or Japanese.
Their social organization divides them
into five classes the mobiles, the priests.
the serfs, the croSS-breeds and the
slaves. All of these classes have this
that is democratic-they form together
the Tuareg family, which holds itself
superior to all the other peoples of the
earth.

forces from their plants to fight the

able area between Berwyn Heights

A barn on Mortimers farm. near
Lanham, was burned down, and twice
the Mortimer homestead became
ignted. but each time was saved by

water with one and one-fourth

boil together for five minutes.

cold water over one tablespoonful
OF granulated gelatin, and let
soak for five minutes. Pour the
boiling syrup over the softened
gelatin and stir until dissolved.

one-half cupfuls of the strained
juice of five oranges, and the
juice of one-half of lemon. Pour
into a two-quart mold and fold in
one pint of cream, stiffly whipped
and sweetened with one-third cup

salt, and let stand four hours.

cream poured on top and then
packed in ice and salt. Always
use a covered mold.

addressed to the occupants of
the front seat-had been: cup
Fourteenth street" and "Back
to the Willard.

The Merchants and Manufacturers

til the drivers learn the new rules. AS

sociation says, the one.way rule has

traffic. In the evening conditions are
reversed. 1t seems, though, that a

should be given full time for try-out.

Goose Creek early today and resumed
their march upon Washington, where
their annual field maneuvers will end
this year with dress parade and a
gridiron battle with Georgetown Uni
versity at American League Park
Saturday afternoon.

reciprocated by inviting the entire
town out to camp last evening, where

community singing were offered by

ton of their uniforms, removing all
stains of travel and shining up ac-
coutrements for their formal recep-
tion in the National Capital. Even the
artillery has been shined up for the
occasion, from the smallest trench
howitzers to the numbering siege
guns.

ten miles, to Sugarland run, where

over a hundred cabin passengers and

about the middle of October, taking
supplies to American naval forces

BY the time the news of the disap-
pearance of Sir Georg Barclays party
reached England, Pansy was well on
her way to El-Ammeh


She arrived there one night after
dark. a darkness out from which high
walls doomed and over them strange
sounds came; the thin wall of string
ed instruments; a tom-tom throbbing
through the blue night; the plaintive
song of some itinerant musician. and
the shuttle of crowded human life.


She was not given much time to
dwell upon those things. Her escort
skirted the high walls. big horse
shoe arch doomed up, with heavy iron
gates; gates that changed back as
they approached. And the flare of
torches showed a long passage lead
ing into darkness.


Into the passage her litter was car
ried with swaying somnolent move
ment. Then the gates closed with a
outside; and she and Alice were alone
with the flaming torches, the black,
engulfing passage and half dozen
huge negroes in gorgeous raiment.


With sickly feeling Pansy slipped
from her litter.





The journey had lasted over SIX
weeks. Under other circumstances
Pansy would have enjoyed it. 1t
could not have been more comfort
able. She had travelled in the cool
of the morning and in the cool of
the evening. Always for the long
midday halt the same sumptuouS tent
was up. awaiting her reception. taken
down again after she had departed
and up again before she arrived at
the next hating place.


The country she travelled through
was an interesting one, park-like and
grassy at first, as the weeks passed
becoming ever more sandy and arid,
with occasional patches that were
wonderfully fertile. Until. finally,
like a glowing, yellow sea before her.
she had her first glimpse of the Sa-
hara on it's southern side-billow
upon billow of flaming sand. stretch
ing away TO a tensely blue sky. with
here and there a stunted bush,
twist of coarse grass. or a clump OF
distorted Cacti with red flowers blaZ-
ing against the heated. shimmering
air-a vast solitude where nothing
moved.


For a week they had journeyed
through the desert. Late one even
ing lake came into view. with
where date palms, olives and cluster
ing vines f1ourished. On the far side
a walled city showed.


1t lay golden in the misty glow of
evening, it's minarets standing out
against Swallowed sky. Even as
she approached it had been swallowed
by darkness. Softly the lake Tapped
as they skirted it and the world was
filled with q constant Kissing sigh.
the sound of shifting sand when the
wind roamed over 1.-THE voice of
the desert


Much as PanSy dreaded her journeys
end she welcomed it.


She lived for nothing now but to
see the sultan. to plead with him for
her father, her friends, herself. And
she buoyed herself up with the hope
that her own riches would enable
her to ransom them all.


But if she failed.


She grew sick at the thought. And
the thought was with her as she
stood in the stone passage, her
strained eyes on the gigantic negro
guards who had come to escort her
tired from head to foot in rich.
brightly colored silks. and they lit
orally blazed with jewels.


The man who was their master
might have SO much money that he
would prefer revenge.


This thought was in Pansy's mind
some minutes later when she sat
alone with her maid in one of the
many apartments in the palace of Ell
Ammeh.


1t was big room with walls and
floor of gold mosaic and domed CELL
ing of saDphire-blue. where cut rock
crystals flashed like stars. Five gol
den lamps hung from it. suspended
by golden chains: lamps set with fat
emeralds and rubies and sapphires.


1t was furnished very much as her
tent had been, except that there were
wide ottomanS against the gilded
walls and the tables and stools were
large bureau of the same sweet
scented wood, beautifully carved
Three heavy. pointed doors of sandal
wood led into the apartment. The
place was heavy with it's sensuous
odor.


In little alcove draped with cur
tains of gold tissue the negroes de-
posted Pansy's belongings. Then
they withdrew, leaving the girl and
her maid alone; Pansy with the de-
pressing feeling that money might
not have much influence with the
Sultan Casim Ammeh.


Two of the doors of her gilded
prison were locked, Pansy. quickly
discovered. Outside of the one she
had entered by couple of negro
guards were stationed. who refused
to let her pass.


On learning this she went out into
the fretted gallery. Below a garden
lay. She stood at the head of the
steps leading into it, anxious to get
away from the dim scented silence
of the great room. in touch with the
trees and stars and the cool, rose
scented breath Of night that she I'M
derstood

PARIS, May 3O.-Col. Carleton
B. Mccullough, Of Indianapolis.
Ind, representing the American
Legion, paid a glowing tribute to
the allied dead of\the world war at
the conservation OF the Memorial
Cloister of Holy Trinity Church
here today. He spoke as follows:


I'VE stand in the presence Of the
heroic dead.


1.-THE organs note, reverberating
through these mullioned aisIcs,
shall wake the memory Of their
gallant deeds, and thrill the pulse,
and CLINT the eye. The sturdy ivy
reaching for it's crest, shall sym
bolize their noble purpose. This
cloister, built by loving, reverent
hands, shall be the shrine to which
converge the paths of those who
wish to pay the homage due the
fallen.


Their grosser vesture lies IN
Belieau Wood. Romagne, Suresnes.
Their spirits hover through these
vaulted hills and pass in brave ar
ray before unseeing eyes. In SER
ried lines they sweep along with
guidonS to the fore. Come rolling
caissons laden with potential death,
the Gathering tanks, the rhythmic
cadence Of the tramping feet, The
shouldered rows Of FURNISHED steel.
Come straining feathers Of converg-
ing lines Of vans, and rumbling
guns; and overhead the avion, de.
tying Natures laws. Comes then
the scarlet cross against the white,
bearing Christ's mercy.


Left Us Heritage.


"They are the envied ones, ours
ID the heritage. They left the
forge, the plough, the counting
room, the school, and marched
away because bugle blew. A bugle
sounded from the western front
and every vibrant chord in every
heart responded to the call. They
followed 1t across the traclxless seas,
nor lost its echo In the rushing
storm. They followed 1t through
weary desolate miles where ruined
towns and devastated fields bespoke
their need.


"They lay amidst the tangled
wire along the battle marg6 and
heard it still. The fingered light
against the cloud, the mud, the
Grassland then the dark! But
still 1t echoed in their soundless
ears, the bugle call of human rights.
STONE WALLS TO SPEAK.


80 come we here to do them
lasting honor. This chiselled stone
shall stand when empires die. The
generations pass and memory grows
dim; the yellow parchment curls
and fades; the written page is|
tinctured oft with guile. The truth
full stone alone remains through
centuries to tell the story Of their
sacrifice.


Gods mercy take them all. The
flower of France, and England's
best, and Belgium's brave, and
Italy's Alpine sons, and all that
gallant company. extend their arms
to greet these noble souls who gave
their ell supremely. And when in
after years our cbildren's children
come in reverence to learn the
deathless story craven here, these
living walls shall speak"

ged the waters for more than a

dren were accustomed to play,

combed by searchers led by Billy
Sandford, five-year- brother of

ed the downtown section, without
result.

SALINAS, Cal, Julyy 18.-"Buck.

Upward of 100 man-bating tulls

horses will be conquered, and all
the sports and games and festivities
of Spanish California will be In
dulged. The California rodeo, held
each year in Salinas in July, is a.
development of the rodeos held Tor
more than one hundred years on the
estates Of the early California Span
ish and Mexican families. Combin-
ing business with pleasure, the ro-
deos lasted sometimes a week, some
times two.


Old Spanish Fete. =


The hidalgos, with following OF
picked vaqueres and their remudas
of blooded saddle horses, would as
semble at a certain ranch, round up
the cattle from the neighboring hills,
drive them into great corral, rope
and throw them, brand and ear-mark
them and apportion them among the
various owners, then drive them
away to their respective holdings. q


Every bodied man assisted in
the serious. often dangerous, ''usl-
ness of working the cattle. The
evenings during the rodeo were. given
over to dancing and feasting. Steers
6nV L lie
tillas baked on bot stones, frijoles,
enchiladas and tamales prepared, and
all washed down with vino colorado
or aguardiente.

ing, and, to the clicking of the cas-
tanets and the tinkle of mandolin
and guitar, don and duenna and the
men and women and young people
of their haciendas danced the fan
dango, the Jota Manzanillo, cachucha
and Valses.


Custom Preserved.


This custom and all the gayety
and grace and beauty Of early Cali
fornia are preserved and exempli-
fled to the world in the California
rodeo and Salinas big week. The
wild horse races, bronco busting,
bull riding, bull batting and other
features are thrilling and often ex-
tremely dangerous. Horses that
never have known the feel even of
halter or restraining rope, GCur-
year-old bulls that have been mon
archs in their own domain and are
peeved and provoked when cowboys
assail their dignity and attempt to
ride them never submit without a
terrific battle. The air is filled with
the yipping OF cowboys, the blare of
brass bands. the cheering of the null
titude as skillful riders stick to the
saddle despite the bucking, kicking
and rolling Of Infatuated outlaws.


1t is great spectacle, a great
sport, and from the Sur to the San
Carpojo, from the Moro Colo to Mil
pitas the cowboys and cowgirls of
this great cow country are here for
the event of the year.

tons, is returning to normal. This

and Free State troops was fought in

Two Republicans were killed and
several wounded. The Free Staters
did not report any casualties. The
city hall was attacked simultaneous
ly with the Bank of Ireland.


Most of the rebels escaped.


Fighting began when the irreg-

Free State troops were rushed to

irregulars had taken shelter behind
barricades.


The violent volleys of shots that
followed threw the entire center
Of the city into panic.


Irregulars took up positions on
roof tops and fired upon passing
Free State soldiers. The latter
rushed into the buildings firing as
they ran.


Rebels entered government build
ings and started fires, but they were
extinguished by firemen before they
did serious damage.


A Gordon of Free State troops
was thrown about that section OF
the city where fighting was most
severe.

vessel.

rescue. He was dragged under twice
by the stewards weight. Patrolman

water and helped Mcneil pull
Halleck ashore.

when the steward slipped and many
passengers who lined the rail wit
messed the rescue. Mcneil has
been recommended for a Congress
sional medal for life-saving.

COBLENZ. January l3.-The Amer
ican transport St. Mihiel will look a
good deal like Noah's ark when she
sails from Antwerp with the last of
the American forces in Germany If
the officers and men are allowed to
carry all the queer animals and mer-
chandise they have accumulated in
the idle and fauciful hours of the last
four years.


The extent and variety of these pos
sessions only began to dawn upon
them during their hurried prepara-
tions for the homeward voyage, and
some are expressing the fear that
their menagerie will have to be left
on the Rhine.


The men have acquired many
strange creatures. ranging from mon
keys to Rhine fish. The exact num-
ber of German police dogs in the out
fit is unknown, but they are multi
tude, and, in addition. there are nu-
merous dachshunds, turtles. monkeys
and song birds.


or the inanimate objects there are
queer little music boxes fixed in the
bottom of beer stems that when
properly worked, make noises like
birds; there are weird collections of
post cardS, antique pictures ana All
varieties of carved pipes, and great
supplies of carpets and civilian
clothes, the latter including queer
shaped hats and silk underwear,
bought at ridiculously low prices in
Cologne, together with furs and other
odds and ends.


Fifty Remain Behind.


There will remain for a time fifty
officers and men to straighten out
the records, dispose of property and
settle claims. Maj. Gen. Allen and
Col. William w. Harris, chief of staff
of the army of occupation, probably
will head this rear guard. They will
close down the model farm, where
cattle, hogs, chickens. rabbits, fruits
and vegetables have been raised and
to which was attached a large dairy.


Then, too, there are a number of
Army schools, tennis courts, golf clubs
and an athletic field near Fort Alex
andria where polo matches were held
and where American horsemanship
frequently prevailed over that of the
allied soldiers in high jumping COM
petition.


One place which officers and men
will abandon with great regret is
Carnival Island, the scene of many
horse shows and base ball and foot
ball matches.

Fourteen-year-ol Margaret Candida

land sound to obtain aid for her
twelve-year- brother. a twelve
year-old girl chum and two school
teachers who were adrift In row
boat. It was learned after they had
been picked up off Port Jefferson.

an oar when mile from shore. They
were clad in bathing suits. and Miss
Candida plunged overheard to recover
the oar. The boat drifted away be-
fore a stiff wind and when she saw
she could not get back to 1T with the
oar she calmly set out for shore.
which she reached exhausted after a
two-hour battle with strong currents.
She was able to tell her story, and
soon many boats were searching for
the drifting boat. 1t was found by
fishermen.


The teachers. Misses Caroline Spar
no and Mary Rich. said a storm almost
capsized the drifting boat and all
took turns at bailing out the shipped
water. Several sound steamers passed
them. but their calls for assistance
were unheard.


Miss Sparno said that at last the
party knelt in the storm tossed craft
and invoked divine help. Soon after
ward the fishermen who had Joined
the searching parties saw the boat
and towed it ashore.

Special Dispatch to The Star.


RIVERDALE, Md, May l4-An
open switch near the Riverdale sta
ton stopped traffic yesterday on the
Baltimore and Ohio railroad for four
hours. From 4 to 8 pm. a blockade
of two huge freight cars and a
caboose was complete. The tracks
were not cleared until the arrival of
wrecking crews from the Baltimore
and Ohio and PENNSYLVANIA railroads.


A long string of freight cars had
been run in on siding only far
enough to clear the northbound main
track. An engine was switching a
caboose attached to twenty-five cars
when 1t struck the open switch and
crashed into the other cars. Two
wrecking crews arrived simuIta- :
neously. lifting the freight cars and
caboose into the ditch. Long lines
of local passenger trains on both
sides of the wreck were released.
Through passenger trains were routed
over the Pennsylvania railroad. Just
before the accident the New York
fast mail, which travels sixty miles
an hour through this place, passed
the switching engine and freight
cars. No one was injured.

BY the Associated Press.


FREMONT, Ohio, January S.-Ten
persons were injured, two seriously,
when a limited Lake Shore electric
train bound from Cleveland to Toledo
and Detroit crashed. into a stalled
motor truck five miles west of here
last night.


The first car of the train, after
striking a trailer of the truck, turned
over into the ditch, pitching its sixty
passengers into a scrambled heap in
the car. They were released when
farmers cut hole in the roof of
the car.


The second car, containing about
sixty more passengers, did not leave
the rails.


Two passengers on the first car
were seriously hurt and may die. They
are William Helm. seventy years old,
Fremont. and Matilda Cizen, twenty
fve, of Detroit, Mich.


Eight other persons were being
treated at a local hospital for minor
injuries.

NEW YORK, June 1S.-The oldest
iron mines in the United States
have just been closed at Sterling
ton, N. Y. They have been in con-
tinuous operation since 1850, and
ore taken from them was used
to forge the famous chain that
was stretched across the Hudson
river in the revolutionary war to
block British warships. They have
furnished iron for every war the
country has fought.


They were sold last week by the
Pierson family, which has owned
them for many years. Gangs of
men have been at work flooding
the tunnels, demolishing the rail-
road tracks and the buildings. The
reason for this is not known, nor
was the name of the buyer re-
vealed.


Old residents say that the ore
which came from the Ramapo
mountains was useful in making
a particular kind Of steel, and now
that the Sterlington mines are no
longer operating the price Of this
steel will go up.
